title: Kumar v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)
frame:
Forum: Federal Court.
Parties as styled: applicant = SEEMA KUMAR; respondent = THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): Seema Kumar (Applicant), is a citizen of India and seeks judicial review of a decision denying her temporary resident visa (TRV or Visitor Visa) application.
How the layers nest here: The judge is the author (layer 1). The applicant and respondent in this proceeding make submissions to the judge (layer 2). The decision under review was made by an earlier decision-maker (layer 3), and that decision may itself report what a claimant, the Minister or a witness said to that decision-maker (layer 4).

paragraphs.text: The Applicant, Ms. Seema Kumar (Applicant), is a citizen of India and seeks judicial review of a decision denying her temporary resident visa (TRV or Visitor Visa) application. On December 19, 2024, the immigration officer (Officer) rejected the application because they were not satisfied that the purpose of the visit was temporary and that the Applicant’s assets and financial situation were sufficient to support the proposed travel.

The Applicant wished to visit Canada for approximately one month to see her sister in Montreal and to attend her nephew’s baptism ceremony. To support her application, the Applicant submitted bank statements of 11 accounts covering a period beyond the required six months. She also provided evidence of her newly established real estate business in the form of a business licence, copies of her tax and financial statements, and a lease agreement for a property that generates rental income. Her sister, a Canadian citizen, had also provided evidence of her income and available funds, as well as an invitation letter in which she undertook to provide accommodation and other support during the Applicant’s stay.
Additionally, the Applicant submitted evidence that she lived with her elderly mother and her brother, as well as evidence of her role and connection to her mother.

Ultimately, in rejecting the TRV application, the Officer noted the following in the Global Case Management System (GCSM) notes, which constitute part of their reasons: I have reviewed the application. The purpose of your visit to Canada is not consistent with a temporary stay given the details you have provided in the application. The applicant does not have significant family ties outside Canada. I am not satisfied with the proof of funds demonstrated by the PA. Although financial documentation has been provided showing available funds, there is insufficient evidence regarding the origin of these funds. Considering this factor, I am not satisfied that the PA is sufficiently established and has the financial ability to justify such travel expenses. Taking the applicant's travel plan into account, the documentation provided in support of the applicant's financial situation does not demonstrate that funds would be sufficient or available. I am not satisfied that the proposed stay would be a reasonable expense. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the applicant meets the requirements of the Act and/or the Regulations, and would depart Canada at the end of authorized stay.
For the following reasons, I grant the Applicant’s judicial review. I find that the decision was unreasonable.
I agree with the parties that the main issue is whether the Officer’s decision was reasonable.
paragraphs.heading_before: III. The Issues and Standard of Review

paragraphs.text: The standard of review applicable to visa decisions is reasonableness (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 23 [Vavilov]; Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1645 at para 13; Shah v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1741 at para 15). A reasonable decision is “based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis” and “is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Vavilov at para 85). The reviewing court must ensure that the decision is justifiable, intelligible, and transparent (Vavilov at para 95). Justifiable and transparent decisions account for central issues and concerns raised in the parties’ submissions to the decision maker (Vavilov at para 127).

The Applicant also raised procedural fairness as an issue. Since I find the decision to be unreasonable, I need not deal with the procedural fairness arguments, or the standard of review governing it. IV. Analysis A. The Officer’s decision was unreasonable
The decision is unreasonable as it does not grapple with the evidence that directly contradicts the Officer’s findings.

I understand that on a TRV application, the Applicant must establish that they meet the requirements of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001 c 27 (IRPA) and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 (IRPR). Visa officers have a wide discretion in their assessment of the application and the Court ought to provide considerable deference to an officer’s decision given the level of expertise they bring to these matters (Chera v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 733 at para 36 and Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1745 at para 14). The onus is on the Applicant who seeks temporary entry to Canada to establish and satisfy a visa officer that they will leave Canada at the end of the authorized period of stay.

In addition, in assessing the reasonableness of the decision, the Court recognizes that the high volume of visa decisions and the relatively limited consequences of a refusal are such that extensive reasons are not required (Vavilov at paras 88, 91; Lingepo v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 552 at para 13; Yuzer v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 781 at paras 9, 16 [Yuzer]; Wang v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1298 at paras 19–20). Nonetheless, the reasons given by the Officer must, when read in the context of the record, adequately explain and justify why the application was refused (Yuzer at paras 9, 20; Hashemi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1562 at para 35; Vavilov at paras 86, 93–98). When there is contradictory evidence, the Officer must explain how they reached a contrary conclusion in light of that evidence (Seyedsalehi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1250 [Seyedsalehi]).
In this case, there was evidence that contradicted the conclusion and I find that the Officer did not grapple with such evidence.

The Applicant’s evidence that contradicted the Officer’s findings, as mentioned above, included significant long-term bank statements showing ongoing deposits as source of funds. They totalled 5,534,658.16 Indian rupees, which the Applicant estimated to be equivalent to more than CAD $90,000. The documents provided also included evidence of business activities, financial statements, and her leasehold agreement demonstrating rental income. The Applicant’s host sister also provided a detailed invitation letter explaining her financial undertaking, which was substantiated by her tax returns and statements of assets in a Canadian bank account with over CAD $215,000. The sister provided relevant context that the Officer was required to consider when assessing the Applicant’s financial circumstances and travel plans.

Although the Applicant is a single woman and wanted to visit her sister in Canada, she presented evidence that her other immediate family members, namely her brother and mother reside in India, as well as evidence of her relationship to her mother and her mother’s dependence on her. While it is not for this Court to weigh that evidence, it was the Officer’s role to do so, and they failed to engage with it.

Regardless, other than listing a number of boiler plate factors, such as not having sufficient family ties outside of Canada, which contradict the evidence before the Officer, the reasons do not engage with the Applicant’s evidence in any way, shape, or form. At the hearing, the Respondent’s counsel tried to point to what they saw as weaknesses in the evidence to suggest that the reasons were reasonable. However, in the absence of any engagement or analysis by the Officer, counsel’s submissions are speculating as to what factors, if any, may have been important to the Officer. The Officer’s lack of engagement with the contradictory evidence created a logical vacuum which resulted in a breakdown in the chain of reasoning.

Given the totality of the evidence before the Officer, there is nothing in the reasons to suggest that the Officer sufficiently turned their mind to the relevant contradictory evidence (Shirazi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 822 at paras 17-18). By not engaging with the contrary evidence in any way, the Officer made an arbitrary decision (Seyedsalehi). I therefore find that the reasons are unintelligible, unjustified and opaque, and therefore unreasonable.
The Application for judicial review is granted. This matter is referred to the visa post to be decided by a different Officer.

The parties did not propose a certified question, and I agree that none arises in this case. JUDGMENT IN IMM-289-25 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The Application for Judicial Review is granted.
